q: An auditor wants evidence that the duties of opening mail, recording cash receipts, and reconciling the bank account are performed by different employees. This control leaves no documentary trail. Which approach provides the most appropriate evidence of its operating effectiveness?
choices: Inquiry of the controller about who performs each duty
Inquiry combined with observation of the employees performing their assigned duties
Inspection of the bank reconciliations for the reviewer's initials
Recalculation of the cash receipts totals for a sample of days
exp: For a control with no documentation, such as segregation of duties, the auditor combines inquiry with observation and, where possible, corroborating inquiry. AU-C 330 states that inquiry alone is not sufficient to test operating effectiveness. Inspecting reconciliation initials tests a different control.

q: To test a credit approval control, an auditor selects a sample of approved sales orders, independently obtains each customer's credit limit and outstanding balance at the order date, and determines whether the approval was appropriate under company policy. This procedure is best described as
choices: inspection
observation
inquiry
reperformance
exp: Reperformance means the auditor independently executes the control to see whether it was performed properly. It provides stronger evidence than inspecting for approval initials, which shows only that someone signed, not that the approval was appropriate.

q: An auditor tested the operating effectiveness of controls over purchasing as of September 30 and plans to rely on them for the year ending December 31. Under AU-C 330, the auditor should
choices: make no further inquiry, because interim testing covers the entire year
retest the controls as of December 31 using the same sample size
obtain evidence about significant changes to the controls after the interim date and determine what additional evidence is needed for the remaining period
assess control risk at the maximum for the fourth quarter
exp: When controls are tested at an interim date, AU-C 330 requires the auditor to obtain evidence about significant changes after that date and to determine the additional evidence needed for the remaining period. That judgment considers factors such as the significance of the RMM, the length of the remaining period, and the control environment. A full retest is not automatically required.

q: An auditor tested a manual control over payroll rate changes in the prior-year audit. The control does not address a significant risk. In the current year, inquiry combined with inspection of documentation shows that the control has not changed. Under AU-C 330, the auditor
choices: may rely on the prior-year evidence, provided each such control is tested at least once in every third audit and some controls are tested in each audit
must retest the control in the current year, because evidence from prior audits cannot be used
may rely on the prior-year evidence indefinitely as long as the control remains unchanged
may rely on the prior-year evidence only if management represents in writing that the control is unchanged
exp: AU-C 330 allows evidence from prior audits for unchanged controls not addressing significant risks if continuing relevance is established. Such controls must be tested at least once every third audit, with some controls tested in each audit. Indefinite reliance and reliance on representations alone are not permitted.

q: An auditor plans to rely on controls over revenue recognition for a contract type the auditor has identified as a significant risk. The same controls were tested last year and have not changed. Under AU-C 330, the auditor
choices: may rely on last year's test, because the controls have not changed
may rely on last year's test if this is not the third consecutive audit
must test the operating effectiveness of those controls in the current period
need not test the controls, because significant risks are addressed only by substantive procedures
exp: AU-C 330 prohibits relying on evidence from previous audits for controls that mitigate a significant risk. If the auditor relies on those controls, they must be tested in the current period. Significant risks may be addressed partly through controls, so it is wrong to say that only substantive procedures apply.

q: From a sample of cash disbursement vouchers, an auditor examines each voucher for evidence of approval by an authorized manager and also agrees the amount paid to the vendor invoice and receiving report. This approach is best described as
choices: a test of controls only
a dual-purpose test
a substantive analytical procedure
a walkthrough
exp: A dual-purpose test uses the same items to test a control (approval) and to perform a test of details (agreeing amounts). The sample must be large enough to meet the objectives of both tests. A walkthrough follows one or a few transactions through the process to confirm understanding.

q: While testing approval of journal entries, an auditor finds one deviation: the controller bypassed the required CFO approval to post a large entry that reduced an accrued liability, and the controller cannot explain why. How should the auditor treat this deviation?
choices: Evaluate it only by including it in the computed sample deviation rate
Disregard it, because one deviation in a sample is within the expected rate
Replace the item with another selection, because the deviation was unusual
Consider its qualitative implications, including possible fraud and management override, beyond its effect on the deviation rate
exp: AU-C 530 and AU-C 240 require the auditor to consider the nature and cause of deviations. An apparently intentional override by management may indicate fraud and affect the risk assessment and the reliability of representations, regardless of the deviation rate. Replacing the item would hide the problem.

q: Under PCAOB AS 2201, an auditor tested an automated control that calculates sales discounts and established a baseline in a prior year. In the current year, which condition allows the auditor to use a benchmarking strategy rather than retesting the control's operation?
choices: IT general controls, including program change controls, are effective and the auditor verifies that the control has not changed since the baseline was established
Management represents that no program changes were made during the year
The control was tested in the prior year with no exceptions, regardless of the IT general controls
Benchmarking is allowed for manual controls but not automated controls
exp: AS 2201 allows benchmarking of automated application controls when IT general controls, especially program change and access controls, are effective and the auditor verifies that the control has not changed. A representation from management or a clean prior-year result alone is not enough.

q: A user entity's year ends December 31. The service organization's SOC 1 Type 2 report covers January 1 through September 30. To rely on the service organization's controls for the full year, the user auditor should
choices: obtain additional evidence about the October-December period, such as inquiries of the service organization about significant changes (for example, through a bridge letter), considering the length of the uncovered period and the degree of reliance
rely on the report without further procedures, because nine months is most of the year
disregard the report entirely, because it does not cover the year-end date
request that the service auditor reissue the report with a December 31 date
exp: AU-C 402 requires the user auditor to determine what additional evidence is needed for periods outside the report, considering the length of the gap and the degree of reliance. Bridge letters and inquiries are common sources. The report is still useful evidence, so disregarding it is not necessary.

q: A user auditor plans to rely on controls at a payroll service organization to reduce substantive testing of payroll expense. The only report available is a SOC 1 Type 1 report. Which statement is correct?
choices: The Type 1 report provides sufficient evidence of operating effectiveness for the full year
The Type 1 report is not relevant to a financial statement audit

The Type 1 report addresses the fairness of the description and the suitability of design at a point in time, but not operating effectiveness, so the auditor needs other evidence to rely on the controls
The Type 1 report allows reliance if the user auditor refers to the service auditor in the audit report
exp: A Type 1 report covers the description and the design of controls as of a specified date. Only a Type 2 report includes tests of operating effectiveness over a period. To rely on controls, the user auditor must obtain a Type 2 report or perform or arrange other tests (AU-C 402).

q: A SOC 1 Type 2 report states that the service organization's controls achieve their objectives only if user entities reconcile the monthly payroll registers to their own time records. Under AU-C 402, the user auditor should
choices: ignore the statement, because it is the service auditor's responsibility
rely on the service auditor's opinion, which covers user entity controls
report the matter as a material weakness of the service organization
obtain an understanding of and, if relying on the controls, test the user entity's complementary user entity controls
exp: Complementary user entity controls (CUECs) are controls the service organization assumes user entities will have. The service auditor does not test them, so the user auditor must evaluate them at the user entity and test them if relying on the controls.

q: A service organization's SOC 1 Type 2 report uses the carve-out method for a subservice organization that hosts its applications. What does this mean for the user auditor?
choices: The subservice organization's controls were tested by the service auditor and included in the opinion
The subservice organization's relevant controls are excluded from the description and testing, so the user auditor must consider how to obtain evidence about them
The subservice organization's controls are not relevant to the user entity's financial reporting
The user auditor must disclaim an opinion on the user entity's financial statements
exp: Under the carve-out method, the subservice organization's controls are excluded from the description and from the service auditor's tests. The user auditor may need a separate report on the subservice organization or other evidence. The inclusive method would include those controls.

q: A user auditor relied on a SOC 1 Type 2 report from a service organization and is issuing an unmodified opinion. Under AU-C 402, the user auditor's report
choices: should refer to the service auditor's report to indicate shared responsibility
should not refer to the work of the service auditor
should refer to the service auditor only if the service auditor's report contained exceptions
should include the service auditor's report as an attachment
exp: AU-C 402 prohibits a user auditor from referring to the service auditor's work in an unmodified opinion unless law or regulation requires it. If a reference is relevant to explaining a modification, the report must state that it does not reduce the user auditor's responsibility.

q: In an integrated audit of an issuer, the auditor tests controls to support both the opinion on internal control over financial reporting and reliance in the financial statement audit. Which statement about the period of testing is correct?
choices: Testing at any interim date is sufficient for both purposes, without roll-forward procedures
Testing only during the last week of the year is sufficient for financial statement reliance throughout the year
Controls need be tested only at the beginning of the year for the ICFR opinion
Tests should provide evidence that controls are effective as of year-end for the ICFR opinion and throughout the period of reliance for the financial statement audit
exp: Under AS 2201, the ICFR opinion is as of the end of the period, while control reliance in the financial statement audit requires evidence over the period of reliance. Integrated testing is designed to meet both objectives. Interim testing needs roll-forward procedures to reach year-end.

q: Which of the following would most likely increase the extent of an auditor's tests of operating effectiveness for a manual control?
choices: The auditor plans to rely heavily on the control to reduce the extent of substantive procedures
The control is performed once a year rather than daily
The auditor expects no deviations based on prior-year results
The auditor plans to perform extensive substantive tests of the related account regardless of the control's effectiveness
exp: Greater planned reliance on a control requires more persuasive evidence of its effectiveness, so the extent of testing increases (AU-C 330). Annual controls need fewer test items than daily controls, and a low expected deviation rate reduces sample size.

q: An auditor is testing management's monthly review of operating expense variances by department as a control over the completeness of accruals. Which procedure is most important to the test?
choices: Confirming that the monthly review meeting appears on the controller's calendar
Inspecting the reports for the reviewer's signature only
Evaluating the precision of the review, including the investigation thresholds and follow-up, and testing the completeness and accuracy of the information used in the review
Asking the reviewer whether any variances were found during the year
exp: For management review controls, the auditor evaluates whether the review is precise enough to detect material misstatements and tests the reliability of the information produced by the entity that the review uses. A signature shows only that the review happened, not that it was effective.

q: An auditor is testing a control designed to ensure that every shipment to a customer is billed. From which population should the auditor select items for testing?
choices: Sales invoices recorded in the sales journal
Customer purchase orders received
Shipping documents prepared by the shipping department
Entries in the accounts receivable subsidiary ledger
exp: To test completeness of billing, the auditor starts from evidence that shipments occurred (shipping documents) and traces them forward to invoices. Selecting from recorded invoices could never reveal a shipment that was not billed.

q: Company policy requires a manager's initials on each vendor invoice before payment. In testing this control, the auditor finds an invoice that was paid without initials, although the auditor confirms that the goods were received and the price was correct. The auditor should treat this item as
choices: not a deviation, because the transaction was valid
a monetary misstatement in accounts payable
a deviation only if the amount exceeds the clearly trivial threshold
a deviation from the prescribed control
exp: A test of controls evaluates whether the control was performed as prescribed. The absence of required approval is a deviation, even if the underlying transaction turns out to be valid. The validity of the transaction relates to substantive testing, not to whether the control operated.

q: While testing controls over cash disbursements using a sample, the auditor cannot locate the supporting documentation for one selected voucher, and no alternative procedure can determine whether the control was applied. Under AU-C 530, the auditor should
choices: select a replacement voucher and continue testing
treat the item as a deviation
exclude the item from the sample and reduce the sample size by one
rely on the clerk's statement that the voucher was properly approved
exp: AU-C 530 says that when the auditor cannot apply the designed procedures or suitable alternatives to a selected item, the item is treated as a deviation. Replacement is appropriate only for items that are not applicable, such as a properly voided check, not for missing documentation.

q: What is the primary limitation of observation as a test of controls?
choices: The evidence relates only to the point in time when the observation was made, and employees may act differently when observed
Observation produces documentary evidence that is too costly to retain
Observation cannot be used for controls that involve segregation of duties
Observation is considered less reliable than inquiry
exp: Observation shows how a control is performed when the auditor is present, but it gives limited evidence about other times in the period, and people may behave differently while observed. Observation is actually a key procedure for segregation of duties and is more reliable than inquiry alone.

q: An auditor attends an unannounced distribution of paychecks and requires each employee to show identification before receiving a check. The auditor then follows up on any unclaimed checks. This procedure is primarily designed to provide evidence that
choices: employees on the payroll actually exist and are working for the company
employees' pay rates are properly authorized
payroll taxes are withheld correctly
overtime hours are approved by supervisors
exp: A surprise payroll distribution addresses the risk of fictitious employees on the payroll, which relates to occurrence or existence. Pay rate authorization and tax withholding are tested by inspecting personnel files and recalculating.

q: An auditor concludes that testing controls over prepaid expenses would be less efficient than performing substantive procedures, and no significant risk exists for that area. Under AU-C 330, the auditor
choices: must still test controls over prepaid expenses before performing substantive procedures
must obtain management's written representation that controls are effective
may choose not to test controls, assess control risk at the maximum, and perform substantive procedures responsive to the assessed risks
may omit both tests of controls and substantive procedures
exp: Tests of controls are required only when the auditor plans to rely on controls or when substantive procedures alone cannot provide sufficient evidence. Otherwise, the auditor may use a substantive approach with control risk assessed at the maximum. Substantive procedures are still required for material balances.

q: Under AU-C 330, in designing tests of operating effectiveness, the auditor should obtain evidence about which of the following?
choices: Only whether the control exists at year-end
Only whether management believes the control is effective
Only whether the control was documented in the entity's policies manual
How the control was applied at relevant times during the period, the consistency with which it was applied, and by whom or by what means it was applied
exp: AU-C 330 directs tests of operating effectiveness to how the control was applied during the period, the consistency of its application, and by whom or by what means. Existence at a point in time or in a policy manual addresses design and implementation, not operation.

q: On July 1, a client replaced its manual three-way match with an automated matching control. The auditor plans to rely on controls over the matching of purchase documents for the entire calendar year. The auditor should
choices: test only the automated control, because it is in place at year-end
test both the manual control for January through June and the automated control for July through December
test only the manual control, because it operated for the longest period
assess control risk at the maximum, because controls that change mid-year cannot be relied on
exp: To rely on controls for the whole period, the auditor needs evidence about each control that operated during the period of reliance. That means testing the superseded manual control and the new automated control. Testing only the year-end control would leave the first half of the year without support.

q: An auditor is testing an automated application control that calculates depreciation using the asset's recorded life and method. IT general controls have been tested and found effective. What extent of testing of the automated control itself is generally sufficient?
choices: A sample of at least 60 assets, as for a daily manual control
Testing every asset in the fixed asset register
No testing, because IT general controls are effective
Testing one instance of each relevant type of calculation or condition the control processes
exp: Because computers process consistently, an automated control supported by effective ITGCs can be tested with one instance of each relevant condition or calculation type. Effective ITGCs support continued operation, but they do not replace testing the application control itself at least once.

q: The external auditor plans to use the internal audit function's tests of controls over inventory as audit evidence. Under AU-C 610, which procedure must the external auditor perform?
choices: Perform sufficient procedures on the body of the internal audit work it plans to use, including reperformance of some of that work
Accept the internal audit results, provided the internal audit director signs a representation
Reperform all of the internal auditors' tests
Refer to the internal audit function in the auditor's report
exp: AU-C 610 requires the external auditor to perform procedures on the body of internal audit work it plans to use, including reperformance of some of it, to evaluate its adequacy. Full reperformance is not required, and the auditor's report never refers to the internal audit function.

q: An auditor did not test controls over sales, but extensive substantive tests of details found no misstatements in revenue. Which conclusion about the controls over sales is appropriate?
choices: The controls are operating effectively, because no misstatements were found
The absence of misstatements found by substantive procedures does not provide evidence that the controls are operating effectively
The controls may be relied on in the next year without testing
The controls should be reported as a significant deficiency
exp: AU-C 330 notes that the absence of misstatements found by substantive procedures is not evidence that the related controls are effective. A misstatement found substantively may, however, indicate a control deficiency. Controls must be tested directly before they can be relied on.

q: A user auditor auditing a company's financial statements receives a SOC 2 Type 2 report from the company's cloud service provider. The report is primarily designed to address
choices: controls relevant to user entities' internal control over financial reporting
the fairness of the service organization's financial statements
controls relevant to security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, or privacy based on the trust services criteria
the user entity's complementary controls
exp: SOC 2 reports address controls relevant to the trust services criteria. They may provide useful information, but SOC 1 reports are designed for user entities' internal control over financial reporting and for user auditors. Mixing up SOC 1 and SOC 2 is the common trap.

q: Company policy requires that credit memos be issued only for goods actually returned, as evidenced by a receiving report for returned goods. Which test of controls best supports reliance on this policy?
choices: Select credit memos issued during the year and inspect them for supporting receiving reports for the returned goods
Select receiving reports for returned goods and trace them to the inventory records
Confirm year-end accounts receivable balances with customers
Inquire of the sales manager about the credit memo approval process
exp: The risk is credit memos without actual returns, so the auditor starts from the credit memos and looks for support. Tracing receiving reports to inventory tests a different direction, which is completeness of recording returns, and inquiry alone is not enough.

q: An auditor plans to rely on a control requiring that changes to employee pay rates in the payroll master file be authorized in writing by the human resources department. Which test of controls is most appropriate?
choices: Recompute gross pay for a sample of employees using current pay rates
Compare total payroll expense with the prior year
Observe the payroll clerk processing the current week's time cards
Select changes from a system-generated report of master file pay rate changes, test the report's completeness, and inspect for HR's written authorization
exp: The control operates on master file changes, so the population should be the changes made during the period, drawn from a report whose completeness the auditor tests, with each change inspected for authorization. Recomputing pay with current rates would not reveal unauthorized rates.
